summary: Hebrew has no verb “to have”. It says that the thing exists “to” the owner: יֵשׁ “there is” + לְ “to” + the owner — יֵשׁ לִי אָח “I have a brother”, literally “there is to me a brother”. With a pronoun, לְ takes the personal endings: לִי, לְךָ (to a man), לָךְ (to a woman), לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ, לָכֶם, לָכֶן, לָהֶם, לָהֶן. יֵשׁ itself never changes. Because the thing owned is the grammatical subject, the past and the future use הָיָה agreeing with that thing — not with the owner: הָיָה לִי מַפְתֵּחַ, הָיְתָה לִי דִּירָה, הָיוּ לִי סְפָרִים; יִהְיֶה לָנוּ תִּינוֹק, תִּהְיֶה לָהֶם תִּינֹקֶת. The negative replaces יֵשׁ with אֵין (אֵין לִי …, lesson 8). Russian and Turkish, which you know, work the same way: у меня есть брат, kardeşim var.

blocks.caption: In the past and future הָיָה agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner.

blocks.title: Having = existing for someone
blocks.text: The thing owned is the subject of the sentence. That is why הָיָה agrees with it, and why standard Hebrew puts no אֶת before it even when it is definite: יֵשׁ לִי הַסֵּפֶר (in speech יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר is very common).

blocks.title: No “I have” verb
blocks.text: *אֲנִי יֵשׁ אָח is wrong: the owner is never the subject. Say יֵשׁ לִי אָח — or, to stress the owner, לִי יֵשׁ אָח.

blocks.title: Have ≠ my
blocks.text: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר “I have a book” — הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי “my book”. לְ is for having, שֶׁל for belonging.

blocks.title: The negative is a different word
blocks.text: Not *לֹא יֵשׁ, but אֵין: אֵין לִי אַחִים “I have no brothers” (lesson 8).

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Who is the owner? (→ לִי, לוֹ, לָהּ …)
In the past or future: what gender and number has the thing owned?

askYourself: Who is the owner? → the form of לְ: לִי, לְךָ / לָךְ, לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ, לָכֶם / לָכֶן, לָהֶם / לָהֶן.
Am I speaking to a man or to a woman? → לְךָ or לָךְ.
Is it now? → יֵשׁ, which never changes.
Is it past or future? → הָיָה / הָיְתָה / הָיוּ or יִהְיֶה / תִּהְיֶה / יִהְיוּ, agreeing with the THING owned (its gender and number).
Is the thing definite? → standard Hebrew adds no אֶת.
Is it negative? → אֵין instead of יֵשׁ (lesson 8).
steps: Put יֵשׁ (or the agreeing form of הָיָה) in front.

traps: *אֲנִי יֵשׁ אָח — the owner goes into לְ: יֵשׁ לִי אָח.
*הָיִיתִי לִי אָחוֹת — the past agrees with the thing, not the owner: הָיְתָה לִי אָחוֹת.
*הָיָה לִי שְׁנֵי טֶלֶפוֹנִים — two phones are plural: הָיוּ לִי שְׁנֵי טֶלֶפוֹנִים.
לְךָ is to a man, לָךְ to a woman: יֵשׁ לְךָ? / יֵשׁ לָךְ?
*לֹא יֵשׁ — the negative is אֵין לִי.
יֵשׁ לִי ≠ שֶׁלִּי: יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר “I have a book”, הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי “my book”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no verb “have” either: عِنْدِي أَخ / لِي أَخ — a preposition with the owner’s suffix, like לִי, but without a word for “there is”.
German uses the verb haben with an accusative object (ich habe einen Bruder); in Hebrew the thing owned is the subject.
Chinese uses the verb 有 (我有一个哥哥) — the same word as “there is”, just as Hebrew יֵשׁ means both.
